utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, we will now, once again, have the witness brought in. Let us have Lieutenant-Colonel Landry brought in. Mr. Cayley, you are going to remain true to your summary, as you ask your questions? Sometimes we move aside. If the Colonel wants to go into every detail of every month that he was there it will be a very long testimony. It is not that he has to be -- just because it is important does not mean that it has to be very, very long. He has to say what he has to say, the most important things. Try to get to the essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I accept what you say, Mr. President. I have spoken to the witness and actually said that he must be concise. Unfortunately he was involved in an enormous number of incidences. To break it up to what is relevant to the indictment is not easy, but he will do his best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. The Tribunal has faith in you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you are going to settle in again. There you are, you may be seated. We are going to continue with the examination-in-chief. Mr. Prosecutor. LIEUTENANT-COLONEL LANDRY (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Colonel. One thing I would ask you, as discussed, if when I ask my questions -- I realise you have much to say and you were involved in many, many incidents in your time in Bosnia, but if you could be as concise as you can, then we will be able to finish your testimony that much more quickly -- without, of course, missing anything else. I know I ask a lot but it will move things along more quickly. If we could return to where we were yesterday, which was the Busovaca Joint Commission, that is where we ended yesterday. The next subject I would like you to address the court upon is the matter of the relative qualities of the communication facilities of the HVO, the Bosnian Croat forces and the Bosnian Army, and by "communications", I mean not only radio communications but road networks and means of networks being able to communicate with each other in the field. If you could summarise briefly for the court your views on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was clear at the time, in March and April and May, that the tactical on-the-ground situation seemed to be in favour of the HVO troops. You remember that there were a large number of BiH elements, that is the Bosnian Muslims who were encircled, isolated. Therefore, it was much easier at that time for the HVO to communicate with their troops than it was for the Bosnian forces. I remember on several occasions, Mr. Merdan had to go away for a day or two in order to be able to communicate with his units, which did not seem to be the case -- it did not seem to be as difficult for the units and sub-units of the HVO in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just remind the court who Mr. Merdan was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Merdan, at that time, was the deputy commander of the third camp and he was the representative -- the official representative of the third camp on the Busovaca Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He was -- there is a translation mistake, he was the deputy commission of the Third Corps of the Bosnian Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now dealing exclusively with transportation routes, for resupply, could you explain to the court who was in a better position and why control of those supply routes was important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, when you look at the tactical deployment of the Bosnian Muslim forces, you will see that they who were in Central Bosnia were isolated. There were Serbs in the north and in the south the HVO. The major access routes in Central Bosnia were either under Serb control or HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, would I be right in saying that it was easier for the HVO to resupply their troops in the field than it was for the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was much easier for them. Much easier to get re-supplied. You should also understand that most of the supplies or the humanitarian aid that was supposed to be brought to Central Bosnia and the Tuzla region had to go through regions under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can now move ahead to 12th April of 1993, when I think you had occasion to go to Travnik. Now, I see you have taken your notebooks. Mr. President, the witness has a number of notebooks very much in the way of police officer keeps contemporaneous notes. He will be using them to refresh his memory. I have not read them. So, he will simply be using it as a means of refreshing his recollection if he needs to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is there any objection on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We certainly want Lieutenant-Colonel Remi Landry to refresh his recollection and give the most accurate testimony. When I question him I will ask how the notebooks have been used, because there could be a situation where they have been, in essence, read to the Prosecution. In that situation, our position is the Defence would have to have access of them to effectively cross-examine. But I have no objection to proceeding at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You raised an objection; Mr. Prosecutor, have you, yourself used these notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, I just explained to the court -- if Mr. Hayman does not believe me, he can ask the witness, who has spent time with me. I have not read the notebooks for this very reason, so this problem does not arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Let me turn to my colleagues. All right, there is no objection to the witness consulting his notes and then the Defence can cross-examine the witness as to what he has said. It has been accepted that the Prosecutor has not used these notes unless it could be otherwise proved. Therefore, answer the questions, please, that you will be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Landry, if you could summarise to the court the events of 12th April 1993 and 13th April 1993, in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to be very concise, but I will have to mention that the situation in Travnik began to deteriorate around 8th April. That was the time around which the Bosnian Muslims decided to respect the Vance-Owen Plan and the Hotel Travnik began province number 10 which was to be under control of the Bosnian Croats. Starting on 8th April, there were incidents which took place, which included incidents relating to a flag or flags, Croatian flags which had been raised at the City Hall. This degenerated into demonstrations on the part of the Muslims. The flags were burned and there were two Bosnian Muslims who were murdered. Afterwards, around the 10th or 12th April, the incidents got worse. After that, there was an intervention of the HVO police, which took reprisals against those people. They wanted to have apologies. In a few days, the situation in Travnik had become completely out of control and at that point we were asked to go on site in order to see that the situations is really out of control. The civilians had erected road blocks; they were keeping people from one or other of the ethnic groups and it did seem that the city of Travnik was -- that is, what was going on in Travnik was going to get worse and worse and turn into rioting. With the assistance of BritBat, we tried to establish a kind of a -- a time when people can go out any more in order to calm things down. Around 12th April things did calm down. Both the soldiers, the HVO and the Bosnian -- and the Muslims and the civilians could walk around. I could say that at that time I was agreeably surprised to realise that there were excellent relations between the HVO and the Bosnian Muslim military people. You understand that Travnik was on the border -- the Serb border within Bosnian territory, so the relations between the various military groups was excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you arrived in Travnik on 12th April, what was the position of the elected Bosnian Muslim mayor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What did not help things is that those Muslims who had been elected in Travnik were told they could not keep their positions since Travnik was supposed to come the capital of province number 10 which was Croatian, so it was unacceptable that the Travnik City Hall be under Muslim control. So the authorities who had been legally elected were told -- that is the Muslim authorities -- were told to leave the City Hall and to leave the positions open for the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you negotiate with the HVO about the fact that the mayor and his staff had effectively been dismissed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were discussions with Ambassador Thebault and representatives in Travnik. At that time we said it was the Vance-Owen Plan which had been accepted and it was not acceptable that a Croatian province -- that the capital of the Croatian province have a municipality which be under Muslim control. That is what I remember about the attitude and behaviour of the authorities at that time. That is the Bosnian Croat authorities in the city of Bosniak or this province which was becoming province number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The HVO said it was unacceptable to have a Muslim mayor and Muslim authorities in the city of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian -- Bosnian Croats said it was not acceptable for the city of Travnik to be managed by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can now move on in time to 14th April, when I think a complaint was made by the HVO to the Busovaca Joint Commission about the kidnapping of four HVO staff officers. Now, the court has heard about this matter before, but I know that you were intimately involved in these events. I wonder if you could briefly summarise to the court what happened in this respect; your investigation; how you managed the release of these four staff officers. Most importantly, your views about the cause of the kidnapping of these four staff officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This period, as my notes show, shows that there was a protest from the HVO representatives to the Commission, according to which Croatian officers had been kidnapped from the Novi Travnik region. Then afterwards, that the general who was the commander of one of the HVO brigades in Zenica had been kidnapped as well. This was a kidnapping which resulted in the death of four or five of his men. Naturally, after that protest, everything was done in order to attempt to find out where the HVO officers had been taken. We contacted the Bosnian authorities in Zenica in order to get -- to get the right to pass through and to investigate the kidnapping of the officers. At that time, we thought that they were Mujehadeen, who had been responsible for the kidnapping. We were convinced that the Mujehadeen had a special relationship with the Muslim brigade which was under the control of the Third Corps. Realising that Merdan had very specific relations -- that is the deputy to the Third Corps commander -- had relations with the Muslim commanders. In the following days we tried to find the road which we thought that the Mujehadeen had taken, with the officers in question. This took us to Bugojno, which was about -- somewhat south-west of Zenica, south-west of Travnik and during the two or three following days, I was directly involved in trying to go back and see what had happened. But unfortunately we were not at all successful and we were not able to find the Mujehadeen or to have the officers -- the Croatian officers released. One should remember -- one should keep in mind that before this, at the end of March, the same protests had been made by the Muslims, according to whom Muslims -- foreign Muslims, people had come from outside of Bosnia who had been captured and illegally held by the HVO in the Kaonik prison inside of Busovaca. This happened two times with two small groups of Muslims who had been captured. Nonetheless, in May, we were contacted by Mujehadeen. Since I was the only one who spoke French at that time, except for Ambassador Thebault at the regional centre, I am the one who was the translator and served as the negotiator with the Mujehadeen. They had come from Algeria. Finally, we learned that those people had captured the Croatian officers and that in exchange for the return of the five Croatian officers, they demanded the release of 10 or 11 Muslims who were being detained in Kaonik. With the help of the Red Cross and with the help of UNPROFOR, we were successful in having the Croatians exchanged for the Muslims. Since the headquarters for this operation -- this negotiation was in Zenica, the Croatian officers were released in Zenica and I was there at that time. That is the time when they were released and exchanged for the Muslim officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. If the witness could be shown Exhibit 290, which is your final report on this matter. (Handed). This, I think, is a summary of what you have already told us. Perhaps it is in more detail. If you could read paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Colonel Blaskic accepted to release 11 foreign detainees kept in Kaonik prison in return for the five HVO officers. He declared that they were all they had under HVO control."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, these foreign nationals, these Muslim foreign nationals that had been detained, I think they are listed in annex C. Did you know anything about these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only information that we had about these individuals was given to us at the time of the protests that were made in March and at the beginning of April, the protests from the BiH, according to which foreign Muslims had been captured, and afterwards we were able to learn who they were, according to the report that the Red Cross gave to us at the time. What I was able to understand about that situation, because I was not able to speak with those individuals, was that they had been arrested by the HVO at checkpoints on the roads, perhaps in the sectors that were under HVO control, and then given their nationality. The people were stripped of their belongings and captured and then put into detention in the military Busovaca prison. After that, specific arrangements were made with the Red Cross so that these people might eventually be extradited to their own country. So, as far as I know, they did not remain in Bosnia once they had been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it your view that these HVO staff officers were kidnapped by the Mujehadeen as a bargaining counter to obtain the release of these foreign Muslims in Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes, that is more or less what happened, but you should remember that we had -- we had had protests asking for their release. They had not been released and I would have to assume that the Croatian officers had been kidnapped so that eventually these Muslims -- the release of these Muslims could be demanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now move on again, Colonel. This is actually moving backwards in time, because the release of these HVO staff officers and the foreign nationals took place in May. I believe that during your investigation into this matter for the HVO, you found yourself in Vitez on the night of 15th April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. On 15th April, that is where I was. You should understand that around 15th April, the activities in Travnik -- what was going on in Travnik really was very disturbing to us and my task was to try to investigate the Croatian protests, according to which the officers had been kidnapped. Therefore, I went on a special mission in order to visit the Bugojno visit so that I could find the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You have explained that already. What I want to concentrate is on the morning of 16th April you found yourself at the ECMM house in Vitez. I would like you to explain to the court very briefly the events of that day as you can recall them. To assist you, if the witness could be shown Exhibit 291, which is a map which you drew for me, which has had some computer-generated marks placed on it which matched the markings you made on an original map. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The joint Busovaca Commission, for several weeks had moved right near to the BritBat battalion headquarters at the north-west extremity of Vitez over here. (Indicating). This is where we had our residence, so that the Commission could meet 24 hours a day if necessary. Therefore, on the morning of the 16th, I left with our armoured vehicle and with one of my colleagues, the driver, in order to go back to Zenica. For several weeks already we had had no trouble moving about on that road and we could use the mountain roads. That is what we did early in the morning between 9.30 and 9.00. We took the road and, at this point --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are pointing to point 2, the circle marked "2", and you are following the blue route marked "A" at the moment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could spell out as we go along, for the purposes of the transcript, the particular point that you are referring to, the number, it makes it clearer for everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The road in blue is the one that we used in the morning. The yellow road is the road that we used at night, the night of the 16th. Point number "1" is the city of Vitez, that is the location of upper Vitez, that was a Muslim pocket, which was located there and then point "2", which is the point where we had a meeting with civilians, civilians who had been forced to lie down in the middle of the road, and when we went -- when we saw them, we had to go around them. We slowed our vehicles down, we drove around them. At that point, I asked my driver to go back because it was a rather unusual situation, it is not every day that you see civilians, four or five civilians lying face-down on the road. We went back, we crossed by them again and we just did not understand what was going on because I was not in a position, nor was my colleague, to see who was forcing the people to lie down on the road like that. We could see that by the look on their faces that they were in a difficult situation. The third time that we went back the group, it was when we saw that there were soldiers, or at least people wearing black uniforms, with light arms, and they were hiding behind the houses and it was at that point I could say that they -- we were able to see them and I simply asked my driver to speed up and to get away. I have to tell you that the faces on the people who were lying on the road were something very moving. They were asking for assistance. It was a very difficult moment, when we had to leave those people there, when we should have been able to help them. After that incident, we continued, and I have to tell you that our attention had been drawn somewhat by the machine-gun firing -- sub-machine-gun firing that was coming from the centre of Vitez. That is why I asked -- there was anti-tank firing, there was sub-machine-gun firing coming from there. So we continued along this road and when we reached this point, ordinarily it was a point where the HVO had a road block and we noticed that this control point, as opposed to what we were used to during the previous days, had been reinforced. By that, I mean that instead of having the usual machine-gun which did not have anybody right near it in order to use it, we could easily see that there were between three, four, five, HVO people who were preventing all traffic from moving through. We stopped. We tried to speak with those people, and to say to them that ECMM had entered into agreements with the belligerents and we wanted to go through. We were told that was not possible. At the time there was fighting on the mountain road and we said: "All right, then we will take the yellow road", which is the valley road and which goes around the group of mountains in order to get back to Zenica. We were told: "No, you cannot go through, it is for your own safety, there is military operations going on, you cannot go through." At that point we decided we would go back, we would return to Vitez. We tried to communicate with the HVO headquarters in order to speak with the people in positions of authority and, according to my notes -- my notes indicate that I tried to communicate with the HVO commander, Colonel Blaskic, but I was told he was not available. After that, we spent the day in our house in Vitez. I should say during the day there was fighting. At least there was sub-machinegun -- there was mortar and machine-gun firing and the sounds were heard coming from Vitez and from our sector. It seemed that BritBat, as well as ourselves, found ourselves between the two firing positions of the BiH forces and the HVO ones. At that time in the evening, we decided -- we tried to join the Zenica area. At that time, we noted that at point 3 here (indicating), that the HVO forces were only blocking the road going in the direction of mountains, saying that they were not negotiable and that the road had been mined. So, at that time we continued along the road, the yellow road going towards Zenica. Now, along the section 4 which actually is quite close, we learned that it was close to the Ahmici village, we saw that the village was on fire. We came closer and we could see that the mosque had been destroyed. Indeed, it had been broken in half. We could see that there were flames that were lighting up the sky. We had the impression that the entire village was on fire. We continued along our path and we arrived at this particular area. We were able to see that on the road there were four bodies lying there, four dead bodies along the side of the road. The instructions we had received prevented us from stopping to see what was going on and what had happened to those four persons, four dead persons lying along the road. So we continued and we joined then up with the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions to clarify matters: at the HVO checkpoint that you referred to at 3, when you arrived there on the morning of 16th April, were they regular HVO soldiers that were manning that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were HVO soldiers who were in charge of controlling that particular post, that traffic area. It was more than a traffic post. It gave the impression that it was some sort of position that could stop any traffic that would try to go through that point, either coming from the north or from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The four corpses that you saw on the road, did you identify them as military personnel or as civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were civilians, but the image -- I can say that these people were not dressed in military clothing that we knew quite well, neither from the BiH side nor from the HVO side. It seemed to me that they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel, you have been a professional soldier for many years. Can you briefly say to the court the conclusion you came to at the time as to what was taking place in Vitez and Ahmici on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conclusion that I was able to share with my colleagues at the regional centre in Zenica is that indeed there was some sort of military operation that was orchestrated around the Ahmici village. Why do I talk about a military operation? Well, it was obvious that Ahmici had been a tactical objective. Ahmici is located in a zone predominantly dominated by the HVO. So, we would call this a "clean-up" operation. We had established whether -- checkpoints had been established on the road from Amna to Ahmici and more mobile troops then carried out clean-up operations and then actually went to attack the village itself. But the forces we met in the morning, were simply troops finishing up the clean-up job and attempting to clean up and hide any evidence of what had happened at the Ahmici village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated that the entire village was burning when you arrived in the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was quite obvious. We could see that there was an immense fire coming from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it normal practice, in a clean-up operation, to burn an entire village to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not normally. Normally, what occurred was that several things could happen. This kind of cleansing operation, especially for an area of tactical importance -- first of all, you would destroy certain buildings or houses, either those areas that may contain some sort of military munitions, but it was quite usual -- rather, it was quite unusual to actually go ahead and burn a village. It is very difficult for me to say from a military respective, to say what was the reasons from a military respective to carry out such a carnage. Later on we went to visit this village, just a few days later, with Ambassador Thebault and under an armed escort provided by the BritBat from the number 4 forces and we -- then I personally saw that there was no defensible position in this village, in the sense that this village was never prepared either by the Bosnians or by the HVO to defend itself. It seemed to be simply a village without any Defence, which was quite frankly simply destroyed, for reasons which were of no tactical importance. If this village did have some tactical importance, perhaps it would have been for the HVO to be able to consolidate their position and to maintain some sort of observation post or stop post for the military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, in the evening, did you find -- on the evening of 16th April -- were there HVO infantry in the village consolidating any sort of position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Be more precise. Are you talking about the evening of the 16th, when we saw the village on fire; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went by the village on the 16th, there was no military presence that was near the village. Once again, if it had been a military objective, this particular village would have at least have had a military presence, at least to confirm the victory or at least the objective that was at hand. Once again, I like to repeat that at the point of contact number 2 -- I am sorry, correction, point 3, which you see there on your screen, the forces that were there, had been there that morning, had diminished later on. There were many people there before. So, once again, I had some difficulty understanding this type of objective, this military objective was truly one -- was really such a military objective, because normally this is what we would find in that kind of operation. But to see it completely destroyed without seeing any military operands left behind is unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I think we can now move on. That evening, when you eventually managed to pass the valley road, you returned to Zenica and I think you found that the HVO brigade that had been based in Zenica had left. I wonder if you can briefly explain to the court what had happened to the HVO brigade in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seemed that the evening of the 16th or the 17th, there was some reaction by the Bosnian troops at the HQ, at the headquarters. It seemed that most of them had come from the Zenica area and it seemed that some action was taken to stop or to try to confront some of these brigades who were near this opening -- road leading into the mountains. Now, there were some troops leaving from Vitez going to Zenica. These were basically HVO troops. What I learned later on was when we arrived that there were some combat that had been taking place during the evening, particularly on these mountain roads between HVO and Bosnian troops. I learned later on then that several male Croats living in Zenica, the majority of which were military, were disarmed, arrested and placed in the Zenica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 292, together with the French translation, 292A. (Handed). Now, this is a protest purportedly from Colonel Blaskic, dated 18th April, which was received both by UNPROFOR in Bila and by the ECMM in Zenica. Do you recall receiving this document at your headquarters in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think -- and we will move on to this in a moment -- the ECMM actually reacted to this protest and mounted an investigation into these allegations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You should also be reminded that one of the reasons that the ECMM was able to act as a mediator, and one of the things we tried to do as well is that when we received a protest of this nature, we would try, as quickly as possible, to investigate the nature or the character of this protest, to find out whether it was well-founded. Given the fact that the communication systems for radio and television were not in order, were not functioning very well, it is very important then to initiate actions that would help to put down any rumours which may influence either the Muslim or the Croatian population. People may be very inclined to follow rumours, these can circulate very quickly and then maybe it may be important to try to bring things back to a calmer and normalised situation. We found that sometimes these rumours can cause certain people to take up action against the other ethnic groups. So when we received this protest, Mr. Thebault at that time asked that we put together an investigation commission so we could determine whether or not whether the state was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think before you actually started this investigation there were one or two other events which took place. I would like to deal with those first. If the witness could be shown Exhibit 293. (Handed). Now, this is a cease-fire order, purportedly signed by Colonel Blaskic, which is addressed to the commanders of all HVO units, the British battalion commander, ECMM Mission and the Third Corps headquarters. It is the result of an agreement between the HVO head of staff in Herceg-Bosna and presumably the international community. Can you explain what your reaction to this order was at the time you received it in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reacted immediately. It seemed that the orders were sent from the central region HQ and we were quite optimistic because these orders were sent down to the HVO brigades and also to the local units, to stop all activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I know that enthusiasm that you had for this order was somewhat short-lived after you eventually arrived in Kiseljak and saw what had happened there. But, did you actually see any of these orders actually taking effect on the ground at the time it was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must admit that from 18th April, at least for two days, I particularly investigated the situation concerning the state of those villages very close to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse -- sorry, could you turn towards the bench when you speak, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What seemed to be happening is that there seemed to be a reduction -- or rather there seemed to have been a cease-fire but nonetheless my information showed that there was still some sporadic gunfire here and there and there were some reports to that effect. Indeed, we were sent reports on a regular basis to that effect. So, there was an effort to reduce the amount of combat and fighting, but given that all the rumours that were circulating and also the destruction of Ahmici village and some of the activity and some of the Croatian villages in Zenica, I think in my opinion it was very difficult to try to implement this order immediately. I would say then that perhaps the situation did improve, but fighting definitely did continue in a sporadic manner throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think as a result of the protest that you received from Colonel Blaskic, relating to atrocities committed against Croats in the Zenica region, you had a meeting with the deputy commander of the Third Corps, Mr. Merdan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Please understand that to be able to investigate the various villages or to visit these villages, as we were interested to do, first we had to obtain the authorisation of the BiH forces in order to circulate freely. Now, do not forget there were areas under the control of the Bosnian Army. So, in order to go to these villages, first of all, I had to obtain the authorisations necessary. That is why I went to the deputy commander of the Third Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, prosecuting counsel, there are some things I do not understand completely. In this protest, in the French translation, there is a hand-written date and it is not clear exactly what the date is, what the number is. It seems that on the last -- what does that mean when it says "August 1996"? Are these numbers used by the Prosecution or --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can explain it. It is simply when the document was received by the Office of the Prosecutor from Colonel Landry, he signed it and dated it at the time he made his original statement to investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I suspected that was the case, but I wanted you to confirm it. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you minuted the meeting you had with Mr. Merdan and if you could be shown Exhibit 294, which is also in French as 294A. That is a summary of that particular meeting that took place. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received from the deputy commander of the Bosnian Corps, I think it was prepared at that time to make a brief report explaining what had occurred during the preceding days, at least to give this notice to one of the belligerents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think I am right in saying that he provided to you certain allegations of atrocities against the Muslim community in Vitez and Ahmici, did he not, and he identified villages that had been destroyed, including Ahmici and Vecereska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I also admit that a moment ago I did not mention it, but on the morning of the 17th I could clearly see from my hotel room the burnt village and I also could see columns of persons, mostly Muslims, who were fleeing that area in order to go to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you informed Mr. Merdan about the allegations that had been made by the HVO and I think you asked for his assistance in making an investigation into the villages around Zenica. I would like you to summarise in your own words what exactly happened. I will provide to you Exhibit 295, which is a copy of your report, the special report that you did on Croats in Zenica. That is Exhibit 295, and 295A, which is in the French language. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, I will try to be brief, but please understand that this incident and this investigation -- in this case, it lasted more than two days and there was a lot of testimonies. These were not always very easy to listen to, these testimonies and I have very bad memories about the particular events, but I will do my best. It was very important for our own credibility to have someone with us who was able to pass on the information and to help us in our investigations. At that moment, I had heard about a priest -- the priest of the largest Catholic church in Zenica at that point in time. Once I was able to get the assistance from Merdan, from the deputy commander himself, that he was going to accompany us to all the areas we were going to investigate, at that moment I contacted Father Stefan to accompany us as well. Upon my visit with Father Stefan, I must admit that there was an atmosphere in this church which was quite painful to see. Father Stefan had given asylum to several Zenica HVO persons, people who were afraid, people who had heard rumours about their own villages and about the atrocities that had taken place there. They had seen that the Bosnian troops were out of control and indeed it seemed that many crimes were going to be committed. With the aid of Father Stefan, as well as Mr. Merdan, we began our visit by visiting the main prison at Zenica. At that moment there were several hundred Croats. Most of those persons I would say were men. They were all men. But -- most of them were of combat age, I would say; however, there were some elderly persons there as well. Our report indicates that the situation there seemed to be normal, that some of the detainees that we were able to meet with, along with the Father, had some concerns on their faces -- had some injuries on their faces. Generally speaking, people had at least one meal a day. Obviously there are far too many prisoners there for the capacities of the operation of the prison, but it seemed nonetheless to be quite reasonable, for that time period, based on my experience in other prisons. I saw that one man had been arrested and there was some efforts made with the Muslim authorities to release this man. He did not seem to pose any threat to anyone. Indeed, it seemed that was done later that day. By the end of that afternoon, he was indeed freed. The next day or the afternoon, we began to visit various villages. I must admit that there was not really time to do any advance planning. It was Father Stefan who named which villages we were going to visit because he knew the area and there were various villages throughout that area. That is what we did. We visited the various villages in that area, based on the information that the priest gave to us and indicated where we might go. We noted that the area as a whole was under the control and the protection of the Bosnian forces. We saw also that there had been some combat or fighting there. Some houses had been burned. Some people had been wounded or killed in the course of attacks or conflicts. What we saw was not as alarming as what we had been led to believe. We saw Ahmici and we saw how much violence and destruction had taken place in Ahmici. Above all, we found that there were several abandoned houses, some houses which had been burnt. Some also that had Muslims -- Bosnians, rather, and Croats. We had some testimonies given that in some cases Muslims had placed their lives in danger to save the lives of certain Croats, the details are all located here in the report, but it was definitely not what we expected to see. I recall quite well that Father Stefan was, himself, very relieved to see that there was not as much damage as what he expected to see based on what he had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Third Corps cooperate with you fully in conducting this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the deputy Third Corps commander escorted us all through the day and then, depending upon the places Father Stefan visited or wanted to go, I remember several occasions when Mr. Merdan had to use his authority in order to get us through because the people saw that we were being escorted by the Catholic priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the local Bosnian commander, Visnic Neraga, had been given strict orders regarding the security of civilians in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a very clear recollection that one of the first things that we did when we received the allegations as to the HVO protest that Mr. Thebault went to speak to the commander of the Third Corps and it was his responsibility to ensure, as the military chief, to ensure the security and safety of the people and all the civilians who were within the territory under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were those orders given by the Third Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that they came from him and since -- as the report says, during one of the visits during the investigation, we arrived on site and we were able to see that there were bandits at work who were looting the houses and on one very specific occasion we saw special police Third Corps elements who were arresting certain individuals who were looting. Therefore, I could assume that orders had been given to the lowest echelon and measures had been taken in respect of the situation, at least in order to try to reduce as much as possible this type of activity. After that, we noticed that other types of actions taken by the Third Corps leaders -- we should understand at that point, everybody was wearing military uniforms, it was easy for somebody to take a uniform and commit a crime and then possibly one would say it was the HVO or the BiH who had done the crime because the uniform had been seen. At that time the Third Corps decided to initiate a system of identity cards. All of the Bosnian units had an identifying card and each one had shoulder badges which indicated clearly that this individual was working with the Third Corps, so that better control could be exercised over the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 296, please. (Handed). Can you just confirm, Colonel, that these are, in fact, the villages you visited with Mr. Merdan and Father Stefan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are the villages. These are the ones which we reported on in our written report. All we did was to repeat the names of the villages. Then we took a map of Zenica and we indicated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, finally on this point, any person's death diminishes us and there were a number of people that were killed. When you read the protest that you received from the central Bosnian operative, purportedly signed by Colonel Blaskic, and you look back on what you actually saw at the time, what can you say about this protest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could simply deduce that the tone of the protest was extremely exaggerated and that the tone of the protest seemed to want to indicate to the entire international community that atrocities had been committed against the entire HVO or Croatian community, which was under Bosnian control and that it was at that time -- this was another factor used to force the authorities possibly to release or allow the Bosnian Croat citizens of that region to leave so they could go back to regions which were under Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see or hear of any individuals being thrown under tanks in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see one vehicle. It was an assault tank that was moving around in Zenica, but I do not remember at any point having seen a report or a request to go to investigate that soldier -- an HVO soldier or a civilian had been crushed by a tank. But, you have to understand that after a given point, fighting began to the south-west of Zenica. Zenica was a military garrison and it would be natural for there to be some kind of fighting because units would be regrouped there. There was a great deal of military activity going on there, but there were also incidents of brutality committed against the Bosnian Croat citizens. I cannot deny that there were people were killed as well, as indicated in the report as indicated in the report. I do not want to diminish or underestimate the lack of control and the violence that was there, this was unacceptable violence, but in view of the situation, I could simply tell you honestly that that state of violence, even if it was unacceptable, it was not on the same scale as the one we had been informed -- that we had been told had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on the subject of the violence that you saw had taken place in Ahmici and the on-going military operations in Vitez, were you provided with assistance by the HVO to make a full investigation of what had taken place in Vitez on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several investigations carried out subsequently, but I can tell you that in the next few days I went to visit Ahmici. This had to be done with the BritBat armed escort. I have a very clear memory of this. We were not able to go in as we liked, that is into Ahmici. This was done under BritBat escort, at the invitation of the BritBat commander, Thebault. Thanks to him we were able to visit the village of Ahmici in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could specifically answer my question: were you given assistance by the HVO in investigating what had happened in Ahmici and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you left Bosnia-Herzegovina in August 1993. Did you ever receive a report from the HVO on what had taken place in Ahmici and Vitez and the surrounding villages on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. If such a report had been distributed, I should have received it. As I did with all reports that were circulated at that time, I would have known about them and I would have had them. There was no report, at least that I can remember, that was going about at that time in respect of that. But I have to tell you, your Honour, that during my stay in Bosnia, all reports that I drafted and all those that had some significance about what I was doing, I kept with me. This is why I can tell you this with so much certainty, that I do not remember having seen this type of report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, Colonel, did you see any reports from the HVO on any alleged atrocities that they had committed throughout the Lasva Valley region during your time there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move on in time and if the witness could be shown Exhibit D33, which concerns the setting up of the Joint Operation Centre. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is a document we provided to the Defence which the Defence have admitted into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Together with D34A and D34. (Handed). Now, Colonel, this is the setting up of the Joint Operation Centre which, again, was another ECMM and UNPROFOR broken agreement. I would like you briefly to explain to the court the position that you found Mr. Franjo Nakic in on 18th April 1993 when you visited him at his home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this question that you are asking, is it based on the document that you are giving to the witness? The Trial Chamber has nothing in front of it, nor on the projector. It is an independent question you are asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There is a document available for you. It is related to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that period, as you probably understand, there was a great deal of activity taking place. I was able, on 18th April, to learn that Mr. Nakic was no longer the deputy commander of the HVO forces of the central operational zone, but that he had become the chief of staff of headquarters and that during the incidents that took place between 16th and 18th April, I learned from reliable sources that Mr. Nakic was not at his headquarters, but was at his domicile, that is he was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you spoke to him, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I have in my notes, and what I can remember, because I really have to admit that it is five years ago that all this happened and this was only one episode amongst so many others so I really have to rely on my notes. But, according to them, in my notes, in my journal, it says that Mr. Nakic was no longer the deputy commander but that he was at his domicile. That is the only thing I can tell you. I do not want to say anything more than that because I do not remember, except for the fact that Mr. Nakic was not at his command post, but rather that he was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you draw any conclusions at the time as to why Mr. Nakic was at his house around this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was very surprised because for about two months, we had had very good relations. He had given me the impression of being very reasonable. The only reason that I could think of would be that his commander had simply decided to remove him from his command -- his deputy command post, for reasons which I suppose were military. Perhaps he had not been obedient or perhaps he had -- there had been a serious discrepancy between his opinion and his commanders. You should understand between 16th and 22nd April was an extremely active military period and to see that your deputy commander was at home, or is at home, would show me that something just was not right. The role of a deputy commander is not to be at home in crisis periods but to be with his commander and help him as best he can. Afterwards, when I saw that the -- that Mr. Nakic's name was reappearing and that he was present in a different type of commission, this time it was a joint headquarters, where the two corps were there, that is HVO and Bosnian elements who were attempting to work together and to see that we still saw Mr. Merdan's name as deputy commander and that Mr. Nakic's position had changed. He was no longer the deputy commander but he was the head of the headquarters, which is very unusual for someone in the military like myself to see that the chief of staff is, in fact, to remain with headquarters in order to ensure proper conduct of the operation. Here I learned that Mr. Nakic had the title, but that he spent all day with this -- at this new joint headquarters -- "joint", that is between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this document, D33 shows Mr. Nakic, as you just stated, as the HVO chief of staff on the joint operations centre. Can you describe to me how you found the man during this time compared to when you had known him briefly as deputy commander prior to the events of 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should understand there are about almost two months, every day sometimes from 9.00 to 6.00 we would work very closely with these people, which included Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic. Therefore, I think it was natural that we would develop relations that were not only professional, we would become friends with them. I think that with Mr. Nakic and with his family, good relations -- friendly relations had arisen between him and me. He did not give me any military secrets but we had good friendship. Then I was very surprised to see his attitude, to see his face, to see Mr. Nakic. He seemed to be a man who had been beaten down, a man who had been given posts, but not in a position to assume all of the authority necessary in order to carry out the role that they wanted him to carry out. The events several weeks subsequently, in Kakanj, where we had to intervene in order to mediate between the Muslims and the HVO who were in that region, confirmed that Mr. Nakic had not taken the chief's role in respect of the HVO troops but was serving more as an observer, as a negotiator and there were discussions between Mr. Merdan and the commander of that HVO brigade in that Kakanj area. Mr. Nakic did not seem to me to be the man I had known before during the previous two months, who would meet every day with us as the deputy commander of the HVO troops of the central zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you reached certain conclusions, I think, about Mr. Nakic's views of the events of 16th April. I wonder if you could share those with the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there are several possibilities: either Mr. Nakic may have proved to be incompetent, in which case he would simply be removed from his command. If that is the case, it would explain the little -- the small confidence, the little amount of confidence that the HVO troops had in the cease-fire, by giving us, as a representative and individual, that he did not have any faith. Or for other reasons, having the differences of opinion as to strategy, that existing within the HVO troops, we had simply -- they had simply decided perhaps to set him aside, since he did not agree with what was going on, or with the activities that the HVO was carrying out in Central Bosnia. Then subsequently, unofficially, Mr. Nakic was put back in as the chief of staff, because I have to tell you that we were not told officially that he had been removed -- he had been taken away from his functions, but simply told that for operational reasons, it had been decided to -- that he would be given a new task. But something did happen and the HVO attitude towards Mr. Nakic seemed absolutely incorrect to me in view of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could move ahead to 22nd April, and what came to be known, I think, as the Bilalovac incident. If the witness could be shown the next exhibit, which I think is 297. (Handed). Now, am I right in saying, Colonel, that Bilalovac is on the road between Busovaca and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is about mid point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if I can summarise the start of your journey so we do not waste time on that. I think you were going down to Kiseljak on that road and when you arrived in Bilalovac, you were challenged by a number of Bosnian Muslim soldiers who explained to you that atrocities had taken place in Kiseljak. Can you explain to the court what happened at Bilalovac on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day had ended in Vitez at the centre. There was a meeting with the Bosnian Croat and the Bosnian Muslim representatives, and we were asked to bring some information to people in the Kiseljak region. Ordinarily, we had no trouble moving around in that region, and that is why, as opposed to our usual habits, we were not escorted by the Bosnian and Croatian authorities, we simply had British armoured vehicles so that we would be able to move about safely. We were simply stopped at Bilalovac. We were threatened. I must tell you that had there not been intervention on the part of the police there, we would have been wounded. We were accused of bringing in ammunitions, mortars, to the Croats in the Kiseljak region and tremendous massacres had been committed in several villages and the Bosnian troops who were there seemed to be in a state of shock. They were out of control and there was absolutely no way of speaking with them. However, we were shown a series of villages were massacres had taken place and I can tell you that had the police official from Kacuni not arrived at the time, I would not be here today, most likely, to tell you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibits 299 and 300? I think 299 is a report of your visit to Rotilj following on from the information that you received from the soldiers at Bilalovac about atrocities in Kiseljak. (Handed). If the map could be placed on the ELMO. Could you recall for the court your visit to Rotilj on 25th April and explain what you found there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rotilj was one of the villages that had been mentioned where some atrocities had taken place. We received a protest about that and so we decided, with the chief of operations at the time, to investigate what had happened. Once again, we left in a jeep. The situation was a bit more normal throughout the sector and we were able to go to Kiseljak. At that point, we were not able to use the road in order to get to Rotilj. If you look at the map, Rotilj is a village which is slightly set back from Kiseljak. (Indicating). We would go there on the road through Kiseljak in order to get to Rotilj. We were prevented from going to Rotilj. What we had to do since we were not under escort, because we had HVO representatives with us, we had to leave the vehicle and the elevations and then to go down through the terrain in order to get to Rotilj. Once we arrived, we saw that there had absolutely been some atrocities which had been committed. Specific houses had been burnt, burnt houses between houses which had not at all been set on fire. We met Muslim people from Rotilj who showed us all of the houses where atrocities had been committed. Among other things, we learned that, around 21st or 22nd, HOS troops, that is people dressed in black with masks, who had cleansed that part of the village. Rotilj, if I can show you this, has one part where there are houses. (Indicating). Then there was -- that is a part where the Croats and Muslims live together. There was another sector, more to the south, where, at that time, the majority of the Muslims had taken refuge. We were able to investigate the part shared by the Muslims and the Croats. There was a Muslim house and a Croat one and a Muslim, et cetera. It was cleared that the Muslim houses had been burnt; that at least one woman who was not able to escape on time, who had been raped and then killed with machine-gun busts. The reason I say that is we were able to go into the house where the event had taken place. The house was not burnt, they did not have time to burn it. You could see traces of bullets on the wall. You could see the woman's clothes torn and you could see the table on which she had been raped. On the edge of the road we were able to see what was left of the stains that were on the ground, where apparently Muslims had been killed. There was a head which had been split in two and that person's belongings had been strewn around. We went to visit a house, if you can call it a house, where the people had been burnt, outlawed. Then we were able to see, I think, that it was five -- I did not read the entire report -- the new graves that had been dug. We could see that the earth had been recently moved. We were told then that the other Muslims who had been confined -- at the end of the village and they could not move about freely. That is probably why we were prevented from moving about in our vehicle on the Kiseljak road in order to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think this report was produced by you and I will not ask you to read it. I will simply read it to you and ask you to confirm it. You state at the end of your report: "There is about 600 inhabitants that lived in the south-west part of the village. They are restricted to their village, being surrounded with HVO. They are without electricity, telephone, water supply, and food supply is low. They have an urgent need for a doctor or a nurse. They have children with high fever and no medication. Within this number there is about 100 to 150 refugees from Visoko." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think finally on this incident, there are a number of villages that are marked on this map with a highlighter pen. I think subsequently other Monitors visited these villages, apart from Rotilj and it was reported back to ECMM headquarters that, indeed, HVO-sponsored atrocities had been committed in those villages as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, just for a reference point for the judges, the village of Bilalovac is marked at the top of the map in the left-hand corner, which is where you were originally stopped by Bosnian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not know whether this is an opportune time for you to take a break? It is for me. I am moving towards the end of Colonel Landry's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, how much time would you say you would need to finish with the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Moving as quickly as I can, between 45 minutes and one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then I would suggest that we take the break at 4.30. Perhaps if we work up to -- perhaps 4.30 would be a good time to take a break. Is that okay with you? 10 more minutes, then we will take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are the president, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I am the president, but I am not -- indeed, I am the authority, but we should try to agree, of course. Let us take a break at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am content to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Landry, can we now move forward to 28th April, 1993, and the hijacking of a convoy by the HVO in Busovaca? If the witness could be shown Exhibit 301. (Handed). The discovery of the hijacking of the convoy in Busovaca I think was, in fact, communicated to you whilst a meeting was taking place between Colonel Blaskic, Brigadier-General Petkovic and Jean-Pierre Thebault; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly to the court what happened on that day in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try. Please understand that during this time period there were many efforts made by the international community to try to bring together the parties, to try to find some sort of cease-fire among the belligerent parties but, nonetheless, there were always other incidents which would occur to upset this. This was one of the days on which Mr. Thebault arranged a meeting with the head of staff of both armies and this was going to be located in Central Bosnia. At that time I did not, myself, attend this meeting, but I was there in charge -- an office in the headquarters. I was told by BritBat, who was located in Vitez, that the HVO in Busovaca had taken -- or hijacked, if you will, a convoy of the UNHCR, and that if the HVO brigade did not release this convoy, then they would send in armoured vehicles to force the release of this convoy. I spoke with Mr. Thebault, Mr. Thebault spoke with the commander of BritBat. Later on the persons responsible for the HVO, General Petkovic, and also Colonel Blaskic met and several persons met at that time. I remember that General Petkovic had succeeded, I assume through representatives of the HVO government, to eventually contact Mr. Kordic and also to order that the military -- the soldiers released this convoy to the BritBat in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any loss of life on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I would have to reread the entire report, but to my memory, there were no deaths or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness can now be shown Exhibit 301 and 301A. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is another series of questions, Prosecutor counsel, or is this related to the same incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is another incident but it is a short piece of evidence and I think it will be completed by 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This document, I think, Colonel Landry, is, in fact, an appeal from Colonel Blaskic, a notice of activities -- probable activities of Bosnian forces and dated May 14th. Can you explain why you believed this appeal was sent and how at this time the tactical position on the ground between the HVO and the BiH had actually changed by this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, you should remember that the entire month of March -- actually the entire winter period of 1993, all the way to the spring and even the early part of May, the HVO operational forces were really tactically positioned in the various areas in Central Bosnia. When we saw them -- this is something that would be confirmed later on in June -- what we saw in mid-May was that the presence of Muslims there changed this tactical position. First of all, to the east of Vitez and also east of Zenica, what we could see was indeed the HVO authorities asked us to warn the Muslims about certain attacks which were being carried out or aggressive action, which were being perpetrated against some of the municipalities under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel, why do you think this appeal was made at this time by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, once again, that the international community found -- they felt that the Muslims were becoming more and more aggressive and they wanted the international community to come and intervene and to head off this type of operation. Once again, also to try to minimise the number of lives that might be lost in such an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think now is an appropriate time to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will take a 20-minute recess, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume with the end of the examination-in-chief of Colonel Landry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I would like to have precision about the numbering of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think there is a number which is not there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, document 297, at the start of this document there is a special report about this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 297; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There was some difference in the way the numbers are read in Belgian French rather than French, French.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 297 is a special report concerning the 22 April event. Now, for the document 298 and 298A, this is a special report about the prevention of ethnic cleansing, dated 28th April 1993. At 299, this is a map where there are certain villages which are underlined or highlighted. Then there is document 300 and 300A, they are documents here dealing with the piece negotiations dated April 1993. The final document submitted is 301 and 301A. Here, this is a notice of a possible activities of the BiH dated 15th May. Now, I think we have made rectifications or corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We can continue. Please continue, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Junior counsel finds himself alone, Mr. President. I am not sure why. I am sure my colleagues will probably be joining me soon. Colonel Landry, if we can now proceed to June of 1993, and if you could briefly describe to the court the events surrounding the Tuzla convoy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already stated, you should understand that the central Bosnian region and the region of Tuzla were surrounded either by the Serbs or by the HVO authorities. The main road for supplies that the HVO and the Muslims in the Tuzla area, the main supply route then was the one coming from the coast and was used and taken by the unit of the United Nations. This street went through the mountains. This was the supply route. But, for some reason, due to various controls and other reasons, it was never able to be used appropriately, so during -- or from mid-April, all the way to the month of June, what happened was that the general population was starved. There were fewer and fewer supplies of petrol that were made available. So, all of the electrical supplies for Zenica and also Tuzla was run by coal and one of the reasons that they were saying that these supplies were being prevented from delivery, even though they were being accompanied by convoys of the United Nations and UNPROFOR forces, was that these could be used by the Bosnian forces which could then use them to reinforce their forces and to supply the HVO forces. So, there was a need for supplies. Following initiative by the commander of the Second Corps in the area of Tuzla, following a visit in Zenica, it was heard that the HVO authorities and the Bosnian authorities would send a non-escorted civilian convoy, not escorted by UNPROFOR and not mandated by the UNHCR, to go to the coast in order to buy supplies, food and fuel, so that they could supply Central Bosnia and the Tuzla region. So, around the early part of June, around 500 vehicles went down to Zenica and then drove to coast for resupplies. The convoy had no problems getting to the coast, although there were some problems there and it was heard that the convoy would be escorted by some troops which were controlling some of the territory within the country. But finally the convoy did arrive at the coast. The problems begin only when the convoy was able to reorganise itself because, first of all, they had to make purchases of foods and goods and fuel. These were all done and the trucks then grouped -- or came together once again to return to their original point of departure. I would say all this took around 30 days for this convoy to go there -- correction, took about 13 days to go and come back because these vehicles were stopped for very long periods of time, mostly, and above all in those areas controlled by the HVO, several vehicles were deprived of their contents. Some vehicles were also quite simply stolen. Some people were stopped or arrested, some people were killed. You should see that in a convoy of 500 vehicles, some 50 per cent of the vehicles were able to return to their point of departure. Some of these were filled with contents purchased by civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where did the major attack on this convoy take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly in the Nova Bila region, which is found between the intersection which goes to Travnik and which then goes to Vitez. This is mainly there, I believe, that a large part of this convoy was stripped of its goods and there were about 10 persons or a dozen persons killed during that particular event -- those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was responsible for security in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person who was allowing for this convoy to go through was essentially responsible, so, in a sense, the HVO, if you will, were in charge of assuming the protection of this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was the attack on the convoy an organised attack, or was it just a disorganised group that attacked the convoy in June of 1993 in Bila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the report we received and that we were able to note, because this convoy was joined by teams of the ECMM, we noted that -- we found that these were civilian groups for the most part who would stop this convoy, who would take away some vehicles and also kill some people, including some of the drivers for this convoy. Also, we found there were buses also that would follow along with this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Had the convoy been harassed on its journey all the way from the coast up through Bosnia-Herzegovina to Bila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The convoy was subjected to various stops at various key points along that road. Perhaps I can name a few cities; the city of Prozor, for example, also the city of Gornji Vakuf, where there was another delay, where some cars were stopped and stolen and also there was one tanker that was emptied of its contents. There are other incidents I could name as well, but the place where the highest number of crimes were committed, if my memory serves me correctly, would be in the area of Nova Bila, very close to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned these attacks took place in Gornji Vakuf and Prozor; were both these areas controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were protected mainly by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Had the HVO agreed to provide security in all these areas, ECMM had sponsored this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- this was the only reason why the ECMM of Zenica had decided to ratify or agree to such an initiative, because before the convoy actually began to go to Tuzla and Zenica, there were some agreements made, there were some representatives of the HVO and also from the Tuzla region who had come to meet with the authorities of Vitez in order to have some agreement. Otherwise it would be very difficult to find some authorisation for this convoy to move about, particularly since there is some animosity that existed at that time period. A moment ago we spoke of some attacks committed by Muslims. You, yourself, showed me a moment ago a report which we requested of the United Nations and of the international community to protect the Croats in the central regions. This shows you that the situation was not a place where the cease-fire was being maintained and respected. You should understand as well that the reason such a convoy was being put together was for humanitarian reasons. It was very obvious that the central area of Bosnia, particularly in the northern area, north of Vitez, there were people there who were starving. People there were starving. UNHCR could not create the ability to carry out the convoy. It was strictly for this reason, for humanitarian reasons, it was decided to go ahead with this initiative and to put together a convoy that was being called the "Tuzla Choice" convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that inadequate security had been provided and particularly in Bila. Who was the HVO military commander in Bila who agreed to provide security for the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, it was always Colonel Blaskic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move ahead and if the witness could be shown Exhibit 302 and 302A. (Handed). If I could just make a correction in the transcript. It states that you said the "'Tuzla Choice' convoy". What was the name of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was the "convoy of joy".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not "choice", "joy", sorry. I thought I said "joy".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is moving on to a separate subject. That is the involvement of Croatian armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I wonder if you could summarise this report you received at the regional centre in Zenica in June of 1993, concerning the involvement of the Croatian Army in the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats which was on-going at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My arrival then at the regional centre in Zenica and early March there were rumours that the Croatian troops from Croatia were aiding the HVO troops from Bosnia and their military strategies, either by supplying them logistical means or by giving them units who would come from Croatia. So, immediately after my arrival at the ECMM headquarters, I insisted that everyone working in these areas, whether the area predominantly covered by the Croat and the Bosnians within Bosnia, be able to identify the vehicles. As you know, the soldiers have their own means of identifying their own vehicles, each vehicle could be identified by number or have some sort of code, which could be used to identify a unit, a regiment or brigade as well as an army or a nationality.
