So, we were asked to be very careful and to try to verify, whenever we came across a military convoy, to verify the numbers so we would be able to communicate this information to the intelligence unit of the ECMM in Zagreb. What this report described, I looked at it very briefly, it does state that at that time period, this is the month of, I believe, June -- yes, the report dates back to the month of June, it says that, indeed, there were logistical troops which were operating in Bosnian territory in order to support the operations of the HVO within Bosnian territory. In addition, it was admitted by members of the command within Bosnia that in addition to logistical support there was also an undetermined number of individuals who voluntarily decided to join the HVO ranks. I must admit to you also that it was quite difficult for us to identify the HV elements from the HVO elements for two simple reasons: most of the movement was carried out during the night, which is quite normal for a military operation. You would move your troops during the night because it is more difficult to detect or to be detected. So, these security reasons required the ECMM to also move about in the night to observe. We did not have the equipment to do so and we were not armed. So, we also noted that there were combat troops, we suspected as being -- Croatians supporting the Croatian troops in Central Bosnia, particularly between Prozor and Zenica. This particularly prevented us from being able to move about on these roads. The roads, for example, between Jablanica and Prozor. It was difficult for us, therefore, to be able to move in this area. So, the information that we received from various sources indicated that it was principally the HV troops that were fighting then with the HVO troops. So, with this piece -- what this piece of paper says is basically telling us that indeed there were elements or HV forces which were operating within Bosnian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, see any HV units in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the visit at that time, a little bit later, in the southern region, where we had the detachments with the deputy command of the Zenica command. I, myself, was in Prozor and I was able to see vehicles with identification which showed that they were not HVO but rather that they showed they came from -- they were logistical vehicles. We should understand that in military language, this means logistical support to help the combatants to carry out their work, in other words, they were supplying munitions and gasoline and transportation. Without logistical units you cannot operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We think we have understood that. Please answer the question. Let us try to move forward. I think the Tribunal understands what a logistical unit is, in respect to a fighting unit. Please go ahead so you can finish the examination-in-chief, then move on to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 303 and 303A, which, again, is another report which we will not go through but does, in fact, confirm ECMM views that Croatian Army units were present in Bosnia, assisting the HVO in its offensives against the Bosnian Army. Can you just confirm that you have seen that document before? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them. I even helped to write them. As I said, during a visit with the deputy commander, the DH regional centre -- head of the regional centre, wrote that report later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could move to the final exhibits, which are marked 306 and 307, so, in order to save time, I will not be putting in 304 and 305, so if we could correct the position on that now, which are the two final maps. The two final maps there be 304 and 305. Colonel, in conclusion, what was the form of the military campaign that you saw being conducted by the HVO in the municipalities which they controlled. If 304 could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have 306 and 307.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They have now become 304 and 305. In order to save time, I am not going to put in two further exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Dubuisson; 304, 305. The Prosecution gave up on two of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You are not going to use the other ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In order to save time, in order to move ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. This is the map 304, which has the least number of markings. Then 305 is the same map, but where the 10 or 12 provinces are indicated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are asking that 304 be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will repeat the question, Colonel, because it does require a precise answer: what form of military campaign was being conducted by the HVO and in which municipalities? I wish you to base this on what you saw on the ground and the reports you received both as the operations officer and the deputy chief of Mission in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a -- it was a strategy with two objectives which I was able to observe and was shared by most of those people working within ECMM in the Zenica zone. A double strategy, which seemed to approve of the Vance-Owen agreements and signed various cease-fires because what was being sought was the approval and the esteem of the international community. A game was being played on that level in order to show that the HVO was trying to attempt with international authorities -- in order to put an end as quickly as possible to the conflict which was causing ravages and death in Bosnia. And then there was a more -- much more subtle strategy which, in my opinion, consisted of provoking things. Using all types of methods, provoking the Muslims. A strategy which was focused mainly on all those territories and provinces which had been given to the HVO, a strategy which attempted to carry out ethnic cleansing in which one would be -- or to be in a position to allow the Muslims to leave so that they could integrate the Croatian populations living outside those areas and who were mainly living in the so-called Muslim or Serb provinces. It was also a strategy which at that time allowed us to find proof, according to which there was exchange of prisoners, there was exchange of civilians which had taken place at the borders -- the Serb Croatian borders within Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are the municipalities marked on here with the red flames, are those the municipalities in which you both witnessed and received reports of this provocation which you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly, yes. For the most part, these were the cities where the most important HVO activities were observed. This being done as part of the spirit of the strategy that I have just explained to you, an attempt to create incidents in order to provoke the Muslims to react, then to be completely free to pursue a long-term policy which, for all practical purposes, was the cleansing of those regions of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Predominantly against who was this provocation aimed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The provocation was aimed at the Bosnian forces. The provocation, as I have said, which always was done in an atmosphere of saying: "yes, we accept the cease-fire, we agree that these plans should be put into practice"; but, on the ground, things went differently. Any excuse was good in order to delay the implementation of certain plans. The convoys that went through regions were controlled by the H which should have gone to the Bosnians was always delayed for all kinds of reasons, all kinds of reasons. Then, this finally would lead to the reaction that was being sought. Round the end of May or beginning of June, the Bosnians, in fact, did react.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did this provocation involve breaches of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see through some of the examples that we have discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 305. (Handed). That is a super-imposition of the Vance-Owen Plan on top of the map that you have just described. Are you familiar with the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, I know it very well because, as soon as the plan was approved by the Bosnians, around the end of March, the European Community decided to become directly involved in order to facilitate the transition to that plan. It was at the same time that the region -- at least the Zenica regional centre doubled its staff in order to facilitate the transition. Our role was to explain to the various municipalities and the various provisional governments what the details of the plan were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to the court what this shows and what the importance of the yellow arrow is, as briefly as possible, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The red represents the provincial boundaries, the red triangles represent the various locations where activity had been generated; combat, atrocities, violence against the civilian populations -- the Muslim population that is -- then the yellow line shows the only available road for bringing in supplies to Central Bosnia, in provinces 9 and 7. So the control of that road or the domination of that area by the HVO for all practical purposes gave them control of all of the Muslim provinces insofar as supplies were concerned. You should also understand that the Vance-Owen Plan, even if it was used in order to allow this -- that the cleansing take place, the Vance-Owen Plan recognised that the provinces 7 and 8, there should be Muslim leadership -- 8 and 10, excuse me. Croat. So the Government of those provinces should also represent the minorities within them. Therefore, it should allow the minorities in the provinces to be present at all levels of provincial government.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I interpret you to clarify something in the transcript? Am I right in saying that provinces 8 and 10, under Vance-Owen, were to be under Bosnian Croat governance, but with representation from the Muslim community in those areas, is that correct? I am sorry, I did not receive your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. 10 and 3 were to be under control -- 10, 8 and 3 were to be under Croat control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, is it your view that the HVO made their own interpretation of the Vance-Owen Plan in the way that they implemented it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. As I have already said, it was clear that they tried to do everything in order to get back those Croats who were living outside those provinces and to chase out by any means all of the Muslim population that was there. If not to chase them out at least to demand that military Bosnian troops fall under the HVO military control. Once again, this was part of the feeling which was shared at that time, that had been a tacit understanding between the Serbs and the Croats, so that that part would belong or would be able to be attached to Croatia in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Some final questions, Mr. President. A matter of five or 10 minutes. Colonel Landry, did Colonel Blaskic, when he was commander of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, ever inform you or any member of the ECMM that there were elements of his command that were out of control and conducting military operations without any supervision from higher command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have described to the court a fairly systematic operation taking place across a number of municipalities which you have marked on that map. Is it possible, Colonel, that armed criminal gangs, under nobody's particular control, were conducting this campaign of violence, or was it something more systematic and organised in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, it is not possible that throughout the period that I was in Bosnia, that armed gangs would have been able to take advantage of that time period in order to increase the activity that they were carrying out, throughout that period. I could assume, I would imagine there would be one or two or three incidents which may have taken place that might have been armed gangs but not in a systematic way. You should understand that this plan was done throughout the entire period I was there and this took place progressively.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, speaking exclusively of the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak, with which you were most familiar with the violence that was taking place there, who was the commander of that region? Who was the superior HVO commander in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the period that I was there, the military HVO commander was Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you were a soldier of 30 years experience, you were on the ground at the time. Is it possible, in your view -- and based on your knowledge of events, of what you saw taking place -- that Colonel Blaskic was disconnected from those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two possibilities, in my opinion: the first possibility is that Colonel Blaskic assumed the role of the military chief throughout that period and that he was only a figurehead and that he would close his eyes to the activities that were taking place and which included some of his units, which I doubt very much. Throughout this period, I do not have any hesitation in saying that Colonel Blaskic had the time and as the military chief, should have taken all measures possible in order to ensure that his troops would respond properly to his authority and to set in place systems which would guarantee a certain homogeneity in the chain of command. Colonel Blaskic, when I arrived, knew a great deal about the brigade commanders and his troops and, in my opinion, I think it would have been simply impossible for a military chief in that position for such a long amount of time, telling us for all practical purposes that he did not have control over his soldiers. That is just something which I cannot accept. I just cannot recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There is a clarification, Mr. President, in the transcript. It relates to the incident whilst you were driving from Bila past Vitez and on your way to Ahmici, where you saw a number of soldiers in black uniforms; were you shot at by those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that was why we had to flee. We were fired on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, that is now clear. If I could apply for admission into evidence -- I will not read them all out in order to save time -- in essence, Exhibits 282 through to 305, including all of the translations within that bundle of exhibits which are marked A and B accordingly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to two, we had not seen them before today and I have not had a chance to read them in their entirety, because they are somewhat lengthy, Exhibits 290 and 303. As to all others we have no objection. I would simply like to be able read those this evening and I can inform the Court and counsel tomorrow morning if I have any objection as to 290 and 303. Of course, our lack of objection is not with prejudice to our previously stated objections, such as with respect to hearsay and anonymous hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards hearsay, the Tribunal has already rendered its decision on that question. As regards to these exhibits, they are exhibits -- and we will use an analogy -- and are similar to the ones presented under a different aspect. Do you want to wait to tomorrow, do you want to look at the details? You are a professional, Mr. Hayman, you can see what they are about. As regarding the identification of the exhibit, that is a different issue, but it is not very complicated to see that this was identified by the witness. You can contest its substance, but you know what the case law of this Trial Chamber is. You can think about it until tomorrow if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I make a point on this, I realise you do not want to have lengthy discussion, but this goes back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When there is going to be a debate, there is going to be a debate here. We can have as many discussions here as we like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This whole matter goes back to the early part of this case when the Defence choose, for their own strategic reasons, not to engage in reciprocal discovery. They did not receive documents such as these from us for that reason. That is why Mr. Hayman does not have them in advance of today. Equally, the Prosecutor does not have any of the documents that Mr. Hayman proposes to admit. It is simply ludicrous every time we attempt to put in documents that Mr. Hayman objects on this ground. Moreover, in respect of the hearsay objection, that matter was decided months ago by this court, yet Mr. Hayman continually objects to hearsay. It is something I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you do not have to give me the answer. Yes, we settled the issue of hearsay. Talking about 290 takes us back to a discussion we also reached a decision on. I will consult my colleagues, but it seems to me -- at least personally, I am speaking for myself now -- that this exhibit was identified by the witness. I do not see an objection to having it submitted as an exhibit. It will be submitted as an exhibit and we can begin the cross-examination right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, a few moments ago you testified that at a meeting on 28th April 1993, General Petkovic ordered HVO troops to release a convoy which had been stopped; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said is that General Petkovic was in a position to communicate with the political authorities of the HVO and the HDZ and possibly to have those people, including Mr. Kordic, to give orders to have these vehicles in the convoy released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So your testimony now is that General Petkovic gave an order to Mr. Kordic to release the convoy; is that your testimony? What type of order did General Petkovic give? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not quite understand what is it you are asking. What I do understand is that in my army, military forces are under the control of political people. There were instructions to give communications to a Busovaca Brigade which came from political circles and the instructions, as far as I am concerned, should have been given once again by the political authorities in order to allow this convoy to be released, because the commander of the Busovaca Brigade said that the orders that he had received came from the political wing of the HDZ. So, that -- we were able to meet that evening with the chiefs of staff of the two armies and it seemed that the contact element with the HDZ Government and the HVO chief of staff, which was natural, and that that individual -- therefore, General Petkovic, was able to speak with the political authorities in order to say to them: "You see, we have a cease-fire now, and now everything you are ordering our people on the ground are going against those agreements. Now give us orders that would correspond." What I do not -- I do not know how else I can explain it to you, what other language you want me to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree with what was written by Ambassador Thebault in Exhibit 300?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I take a look at that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Certainly. (Handed). When he wrote, on page 2, paragraph 3 of this teletype, and I quote: "Of 40 trucks UN H0 convoy of food supplies escorted by two Warriors was hijacked on its way to Zenica. The HVO forces responsible for this action claimed that they did not care for the orders of Colonel Blaskic and Brigadier Petkovic concerning the free movement, that they had strict orders from Mr. Kordic, official highest level representative of HVO for Central Bosnia to arrest this convoy and to search it." Is that consistent with the information you have in that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I never said anything different from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you also said a moment ago that there was never a point in time when you had information that there was an HVO element in the Central Bosnia zone that was not under the control of Colonel Blaskic; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I continue to say this, that is exactly what Colonel Blaskic always said to us, even after that incident, I do not remember having -- I do not remember after that incident having seen specific measures taken by Colonel Blaskic in order to remedy the situation, either by removing the brigade commander from his position or taking any measures so that this kind of incident did not happen again. My understanding, therefore, was that given the fact that Colonel Blaskic was not available, and that Mr. Kordic was in that region, and seemed to have a certain type of attitude towards the strategical elements that had been developed by the HVO, he had said that it would be all right to tell the brigade commander to assume that attitude. Once Colonel Blaskic and General Petkovic were made aware of this, they simply went back to the political source -- we were sent back to the political source which was supposed to correct it. Then afterwards, at no point did General Blaskic -- once again I repeat myself, at no point did he say to us that the Busovaca Brigade commander was not under his command. I have always believed that an army is under the political control of its political leaders. One does not go without the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would your opinion change if a commander removed a brigade -- that is a supreme or superior commander -- removed a brigade commander who later came back into power through, if you will, the popular uprising of the troops in that brigade? Would that change your position and your opinion about control of forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are speaking about hypothesis here. What I am saying to you is that Colonel Blaskic, even before I arrived in March, said that he was the commander in chief of all the HVO troops on his territory. After that incident, of 28th April, Colonel Blaskic, once again, and on several occasions, said that he was the commander in chief of all the HVO troops in his territory. Therefore, what that means for me, it means two things: first, that there was a misunderstanding between him and the political leaders and that the situation was then corrected. Or, that Colonel Blaskic said that he was the major person responsible for the HVO troops, knowing all the time that he really was not. Therefore, he was assuming a post for which he was not in a position to take controlling measures. Therefore: "I am a responsible, but when I am not -- I am responsible for the group but if there is something that it does that goes against my opinion then I am no longer responsible." That is how things -- things do not work like that in my army, either you are responsible or you do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think this is all very clear, your opinion. It is your opinion. Let us try to move on to other questions and not go round and round the same situations which are hypothetical or might represent the witness's opinion and which shows that once again the Tribunal has understood. Mr. Hayman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will move on, your Honour, but I will note that in the case of opinion testimony, hypothetical questions are sometimes the only way to test it. The witness did not answer my question. On page 3, paragraph 4 of that same teletype, there is a statement: "It was reported by BritBat that even after the release of the convoy, the local HVO forces continued to stress their refusal of Brigadier Petkovic's orders, claiming they were releasing the convoy only on Mr. Kordic's special orders." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And do you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened on 28th April, yes, absolutely. Later on, as I said, nothing was done, no concrete measures were taken to correct the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, we have heard what you have said and we know what your opinion is on this matter. I would like for us to go on to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could help me, Lieutenant-Colonel, understand exactly what duties you had from what periods of time. For what period of time were you a monitor conducting field work in Bosnia-Herzegovina; can you give me a date? I believe it is sometime in March 1993 until April 22nd 1993. Can you give the exact dates that you were a Monitor in the field, doing field work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must admit that once I arrived in March I was made a member of the Busovaca Commission; I was a member of this Commission until the very end of the Commission, which was around the time period of mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell me when you were a field officer or a Monitor? From what day in March until what day in April, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you give me the time, I could perhaps look in my notes to give you a more detailed date. From the moment I arrived in Zenica, I was appointed to be head of the Busovaca Commission and the role of that Commission was or required that we require of a team in the field and that is what I did until 22nd April. I do not understand exactly what the nature of your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So, on 22nd April, you ceased being a Monitor in the field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are always Monitors. What I was saying is that from that particular date, most of my work was done from HQ in Zenica. There were times in which I did indeed go to the field to investigate certain action, for example, the freeing of those Croat officers. At that moment I continued to carry out my duties but from the headquarters, but, at the same time, I did also get involved in some arrangements in the field for such situations. I do not know if I have answered your question. I do not know where exactly you would like me to go with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it prior to April 22nd, when you became the operations officer, is that right, at RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Prior to that time your duties did not include reviewing reports from other regions and from other monitoring teams; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not quite it. I was a member of the Busovaca Commission, so at that time I had to be able to have access to all reports concerning the situation in Central Bosnia. Even if I was not a Monitor for that particular location, because I was a member of this Commission, I had to have access to all of these reports and, on a regular basis, as I said, the Commission would respond to the Joint Commission and we from time to time would go to the HQ in Zenica to prepare and plan for these meetings and so we had to have a very good knowledge of what was going on within all of the area around Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We had an interview in April of 1997; is that correct? You were kind enough to grant me an interview, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We conducted that interview in the English language; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So let me ask you again: did your duties change in any significant way on April 22nd, when you became an operations officer, with respect to whether you routinely reviewed ECMM reports from other monitoring teams and other regions in Central Bosnia or other parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have the impression you have already asked this question, counsellor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I leave it to the court whether it has been answered. With all respect to the witness and the court, I think we have not gotten there yet. If -- I am not trying to make this painful for any of us. Time is of the essence, but I think I am entitled to an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, would you please try to answer? Personally, I would think this would be for the third time. I do not want for us to violate any of the rights of the Defence. I would ask for the last time that this question be answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to reformulate my answer. If the Defence is asking me from 22nd April I, indeed, had access to more detailed information, or a more daily basis of the information about activities going on throughout Zenica, I could say "yes". But, I must also repeat that during my stay, and given the specific activities I had within the Busovaca Commission, I had access to the same information, but on a less daily basis, and I would say perhaps more on a weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your duties change further when you became the deputy chief of Mission, with respect to this issue of routinely reviewing reports from across Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each report, which was written by the head of operations, had then to be approved by either the commander of the centre or by Ambassador Thebault. So, from the time at which I became the deputy commander -- you should understand there were two levels: first of all, there was the head of operations, the person who made sure there were daily and weekly reports which agreed with our own view of the situation; and, secondly, to guarantee the daily operations of the centre at the HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 283 could be placed before the witness, please. (Handed). This exhibit references a briefing that you received, I believe, in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you find, after you arrived in Bosnia, that HVO forces were organised in a similar manner to the way in which HV forces are described as being organised in this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to reread the document. (Pause). Once again, to understand the nature of your question, what I can say is that, yes, to a certain degree, that the HVO troops, just as the HV troops responded both to the Government in power. So I can say then that the HVO would also have to respond to the HDZ, which was there in power. They have the same commanders just like the HVO, that is true and like the other operational groups that were operating in the HVO territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, in respect to paragraph 7, of this exhibit, 283, it describes the HV, that is the Army of Croatia, as being organised into a regular army, home guards or domobran and reservists, with the domobran or home guards and reservists outnumbering the regular army forces by about five to one. Did you find that those same groupings or categories were used by the HVO in Central Bosnia during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To my memory, I do not recall seeing any of these groups, no; militias, that is. No, not in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does that mean the HVO only had regular army troops or that all of these types of persons were lumped together in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I have a better idea now of the nature of your question. I will try to give you a concise answer. It was very difficult at that time to distinguish between a regular soldier, militia and a police officer or even civilians. One thing is certain, is that no matter what (Inaudible) these people had or no matter what uniform they were wearing, they responded to a very military organisation. This military structure was at all times an integrated part of the HVO. When I would encounter local commanders in the Busovaca Brigade, I saw that these commanders would respond to the HVO commanders. These people were not always wearing military uniforms, often they were residents of villages, but at no time at all did these people lead me to believe that they were part of a different military structure. I would not need to really meet with these people because I was trying to make sure that I applied the cease-fire agreement which had been agreed upon in July and there was also the commanders of Busovaca who had agreed and, indeed, there were orders that were signed to allow the local commanders to follow these orders. Very often some of these commanders were dressed in civilian clothing in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So it is fair to say then that the presence or absence of a uniform in Central Bosnia during the relevant period of time tells us very little about whether someone was a soldier or not; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. That is why I said that the Bosnian troops, from the month of May, had decided then to put together -- or put on a patch, a shoulder patch, as well as have identity cards to indeed demonstrate that they were part of the BiH troops -- BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In certain ECMM documents, a distinction is made between confirmed and unconfirmed information; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, each day we would issue our reports and we would list a number of events and these then would be summarised by some sort of estimate of the situation at hand and very often these estimates were not always confirmed, as you have just stated, but were simply based on our knowledge of the field, which gave us some idea of how we could estimate the situation at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This exhibit, 283, does not distinguish between confirmed and unconfirmed information. Let me ask you to look at paragraph 27, specifically the first sentence, which reads: "The Croatian Defence Council, HVO, is believed to be controlled by the Croatian Army from Zagreb." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that that information is presented in an unconfirmed format; that is, if it were confirmed information it would be presented differently in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I also note the fact that -- I appreciate the fact that you have mentioned this because in the ECMM HQ, which is a strategic HQ, you should note that before such documents are circulated, indeed, there is a great deal of information that must be received first to be able to mention such things and to then send them to all Monitors. Before distributing this type of information, I must admit that all of the people working at ECMM believe this is, indeed, what was happening, given the fact that, missing some evidence, we had to write it in the way it was written there, as you see, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us during your tour of duty in Bosnia whether you gained any personal information that would suggest that the HVO was within the command structure of the HV; that is Republic of Croatian Army? Did you personally obtain any such information during your tour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say that I was never invited by an order given by Blaskic or Petkovic. So, to answer your question, I must say quite honestly, no, but, since I myself was an officer in charge of intelligence, I can tell you that there is some evidence or proof in the field that would lead us to believe that there was, indeed, a link. I would have a great deal of difficulty in understanding and accepting the fact that logistical means would be made available into a Bosnian area for patriotic reasons alone. I think that these were logistical means which were quite rare or usually kept quite jealously in their own HQs and used only in very specific military contexts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have told us previously how the Bosnian Muslims in Central Bosnia had to rely on supply routes that went through HVO territory; for example, in Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only access routes that were acceptable for Central Bosnia for Muslims were those roads which were built -- I say mainly that were built by the United Nations and for which all supplies were frequently transported, but I was aware of the fact there were other roads, mountain roads, and I did, indeed, mention at one point that Merdan, the deputy commander of the Third Corps, did indeed use these roads on certain occasions to join certain units. At times one would have to use mountain roads. I knew that it was possible for these people to get supplies or try to get information in the Bosnian camps which were in the Mostar region because, indeed, there were indeed roads leading to that location but these were roads that could be used to -- were not able, rather, to supply a population of some 5 million in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I was not speaking of Bosnia camps in the Mostar region, I was talking about Bosnian Muslims in Central Bosnia. Would you agree that, with respect to that region, all, or virtually all, of the munitions and supplies that they obtained were permitted to pass through Croatia and through HVO-controlled territory in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me repeat in part what I just stated. I said there were mountain roads that existed which would enable, for various units and Central Bosnia to be joined. But the only road that could truly accommodate road traffic would have to be the roads that go through a sector which is under the control of the HVO. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the Republic of Croatia; correct, in terms of an outlet out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, those roads lead to Dalmatia, which is in the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to paragraph 33 of this briefing paper, which recites, with respect to the HVO in Bosnia, that they are well equipped with both armour and artillery. Let me ask you: did you ever see the HVO in possession of any armour in the Vitez/Busovaca pocket or enclave during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They did not have any, is that not correct? There were no tanks or armoured personnel carriers in the possession of the HVO in the Vitez/Busovaca enclave; do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I said. You asked me what I saw and I said "no".

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you did not recall. Then I asked you: do you agree that, in fact, they did not have any. Do you agree that the HVO, in the Vitez/Busovaca pocket, did not have any armoured carriers or tanks; or do you believe they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I would be more prepared to say that perhaps there is some possibility that they had some of these type of these vehicles, but I am not in a position to say they had none. I saw some artillery. I saw some cannons that were being transported on some vehicles. Perhaps there were other types of vehicles as well that the HVO had in the centre, but that is all I can say. I cannot really confirm this one way or another, whether or not these existed. I can say I saw other types of equipment which may lead me to believe that when you have artillery hardware, perhaps it is not altogether unthinkable to have other types of, perhaps, vehicles for transporting troops and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 285 could be placed before the witness, please. (Handed). This is the ECMM teletype attaching the various 13th February 1993 orders which, as we understand it, gave rise to the Busovaca Joint Commission; is that right? Do these documents include the founding documents for the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is, indeed, it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see the originals of these documents signed by General Hadzihuseinovic and Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them but, once again, the original copy -- I am not the one who had the original copy, but all members of the Busovaca Commission received a copy which I was able to keep over the years. This is what I have here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree, summarising so that we do not go through each one, that this set of orders provided for separation of forces; provision of security for persons returning to their homes; unconditional release of all detainees, other than criminals; removal of road barricades; all checkpoints to be joint; establishment of a Joint Commission; filling in of trenches and bunkers and free passage for humanitarian aid and certain other transport? Would you agree that this set of orders by General Hadzihuseinovic and Colonel Blaskic provided for those steps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in short, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you briefed -- because you were not in Bosnia yet when these orders were issued; correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have to answer audibly so that in the record there is an audible answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I was not there when these orders were written. Indeed, that is the reason that I obtained a copy. Then I had carried it with me on a regular basis to the meetings of the Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you briefed as to whether or not there were any requests by the ECMM at these negotiations in Kakanj on 13th February 1993, to which Colonel Blaskic did not agree; in other words, did he withhold agreement as to any requests that the ECMM made in the course of those negotiations, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not really aware of what you are talking about now. The document I work with is this document here. I did, indeed, meet with two joint meetings in which the heads of the two armed corps were present in order to discuss the situation with regards to the putting into practice of this agreement for cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what ECMM personnel were present at these negotiations on 13th February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone within the ECMM organisation ever tell you that they believed that these orders, which constitute Exhibit 285, were issued in bad faith, either by General Hadzihuseinovic or by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you is that what I did is when I arrived, they gave me information about the Busovaca Commission and then I was told that we had to implement the agreement made in this document, but at no time was I given the understanding that it would not be applicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So, you were never told by anyone within ECMM that these orders were a ruse either on the part of the BiH Army or on the part of the HVO; that is that they had been issued as part of some intention not to carry them forward. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that in the month of March I truly believed, at a moment, that both -- on the BiH side as well as the HVO side -- felt that there was indeed an interest or a will to agree and to comply with this cease-fire agreement. This is what I believed anyway in the month of March. But, as you have heard today and also yesterday, that changed gradually as time progressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you believe that Mr. Nakic did everything he could to see that these orders in Exhibit 285 were enforced and implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was his responsibility, to carry out -- it was the commander's responsibility to carry out those -- he represented the commander and he was supposed to sit with us to hear protests that were made -- that came from the other army, which would sit with us in order to carry out business or to see what was really behind these protests and then make reports to the headquarters as to the situation. Mr. Nakic was not a commander of the operational central zone. He was the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will repeat my question: did you believe that Mr. Nakic did everything he could to see that these orders in Exhibit 285 were enforced and implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March I believe, in fact, that there was excellent communication between the representatives of the Commission and the headquarters. Mr. Nakic was not alone, he was always accompanied by two or three members of the General Nakic's staff and there were regular reports that were prepared. It was the Joint Commission at that time which seemed to confirm to me that the information was passing from one group to another very well. I would like to repeat once again that it was not my perception that Mr. Nakic was the one who was responsible for carrying out the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I did not ask you whether Mr. Nakic was responsible for carrying out orders or whatever. I asked you: did he, in your judgement, make a best efforts attempt, during the time the Commission existed, to see that these orders in Exhibit 285 were implemented and enforced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I can say is that around the end of March or the beginning of April it was clear that there was a lack of cooperation on the part of the HVO representatives; that is, it was this lack of whether it was theirs or whether it was coming from the headquarters, but every excuse was used in order to delay implementation of the cease-fire agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where did these excuses come from, do you know? Where did you encounter them, out in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards the implementation of the communication or the -- that we had to set up in order to re-establish a communication facilities between -- and Kacuni and it was clear at that time that it was not strictly the work of Mr. Nakic, but he had information which would go all the way to the bottom, but it took a great deal of time before we could get written orders from the brigade commanders in order to fill in the trenches. I do not know what else you would like me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You are telling us that, in terms of filling in trenches in the Busovaca municipality, it was the brigade commanders who were the obstacle, because you needed to get the brigade commanders to issue written orders to the lower level commanders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I am saying to you is that a brigade commander takes his orders from his commander, his formation commanders. The deputy commander has limited authority because the deputy commander in the circumstances in which he was appointed represented the commander. In my way of interpreting the works of the Commission, it meant that that commander would make a report to his staff -- his headquarters, rather, and that commander was to take action. That is the reason that, on two occasions in March and the beginning of April, that there were meetings between the Joint Commission because at that time all of the commanders, Halilovic and Blaskic were present at the meetings that were presided over by Mr. Thebault. But, yes, if there is a brigade commander that does not implement orders that were already distributed on 13th February and that brigade commander is a few kilometres away from your Vitez command centre, I think it is your responsibility as the commander to go to verify to be sure whether this brigade is really obeying your orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With respect to the Busovaca Brigade commander, I take it there was a meeting between him and his BiH Army counterpart prior to the signing of the joint order which is one of the exhibits to your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Further to the request of the local commanders, the local commanders said to us: "before we can fill in the trenches we would like to have written orders from our commanders." Therefore, what we did then was we set up series of meetings between the two commanders in order to initiate that procedure. I have very clear recollection that in Busovaca, the commander of the Busovaca Brigade and the Kacuni Brigade came to Busovaca at least one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had the commander of the BiH army brigade in Busovaca, had he issued a written order to his lower level units to fill in the trenches prior to issuing the order which is one of the exhibits to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Because in my opinion, it did not require a written order in order to carry these things out. The only thing that I do remember very clearly is that on the side of the local commanders of the HVO, we would often come back and say that they needed written orders. Military people do not need written orders in order to execute orders, when the orders are at least two months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They should not; that is your point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. As I said, I can remember very clearly that the request came from the HVO troops. Therefore, in order not to create any prejudice to one side or the other, one required joint orders. The same type of order that had been initially given by General Hadzihuseinovic and General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: General Hadzihuseinovic. Prior to the issuance of that joint order by the two brigade commanders in Busovaca, had you seen any BiH army trenches filled in in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What municipality, because there were several?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the Busovaca municipality, which here would be the area of Kacuni, I believe, is where you would be having most contact with BiH Army in the Busovaca municipality. Were any BiH Army trenches filled in prior to the issuance of the joint brigade commander's orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. For the simple reason that before filling in the trenches, both commanders of both organisations wanted themselves to go to the trenches and that had to be done together. This is the agreement that had been reached. So long as one did not want to fill in the trenches, the other one would not fill them in either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I guess they did not trust each other; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So they were dragging their feet together, the BiH Army commander and the HVO brigade commander; would you not say that is a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you. I will tell you why. If I remember the work that I did at that time, both with the local commanders of the Donji Polje region and the local commanders of the Donji Gornji and Solakovici areas. I can tell you at the end, before the trenches were filled, the local commanders on both sides had visited the trenches of the other side and that they were -- they had meetings. I remember that there were at least two meetings that took place between the local commanders on both sides which took place without the ECMM being there. The question which we asked at that point is that each of the sides -- principally on the HVO side is that they want to have a written order before filling in the trenches so that there would be no possible negative consequences to having filled them in. In my opinion, the local commanders already had a certain level of trust regarding the fact that these orders would be written or had been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The orders which are Exhibit 285, would you agree that they were issued --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am objecting at this point, because I think we have covered this ground comprehensively. I think Colonel Landry has answered all the questions concerning these orders and the incident in Solakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am sorry to disappoint you for the first time, but I think that I did not really follow this question because I was wondering what time we should stop. I would like to understand your objection better. First I would like to consult with my colleagues. All right, we will continue until 6.45. I was take -- I was caught in the act of not listening and I apologise and ask Mr. Hayman to ask his question again so I can better understand Mr. Cayley's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I had not quite got all the question out, Mr. President, but I will now. Is it your understanding, Lieutenant-Colonel, that the orders which are Exhibit 285, that they were issued in response to the conflict in the Busovaca municipality which had erupted in late January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Among other things, mainly as regards the conflicts or the violence which took place in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the Commission, itself, was designed principally to monitor conditions in the Busovaca municipality with respect to compliance with these orders; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it was more than the city of Busovaca, at least as I understand it, and as my comrades understood it during the month and a half that I was on that Commission, they did not only relate to Busovaca but that there was a certain emphasis placed on Busovaca. As you can read the essential elements of the cease-fire, it covered the entire operational zone in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 286 could be placed before the witness, please. This is the Busovaca Joint Co-ordination Commission Charter. (Handed). I would direct your attention to the second paragraph, which begins -- it is titled "Aim" and it begins: "The aim of the Busovaca Joint Co-ordination Commission is to monitor and record the situation in the Busovaca area pertaining to compliance of the joint orders issued by the joint command BiH/HVO." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no problem with this. I would just tell you that you should look at who signed this and to see that this document was principally done for the British, I did not answer to the chain of command of General Stewart but rather the ECMM chain of command. This document was presented in order to give an idea of the structure of the Commission. But look at who signed the document and who did not sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You are saying that that might have been BritBat's view, but it was not the ECMM's view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not what I am saying. What I am saying is that it was very important for BritBat, it was very important for BritBat, to normalise the situation in Busovaca, it was their operational centre. BritBat had nothing at all to do in the Kiseljak region, which was under CanBat; BritBat had nothing to do in the Kakanj area which was under the FrenchBat. On several occasions we had to intervene in the Visoko region and in the Kakanj region either with French or with Canadians. Once again, I cannot tell you that this was -- we went against what BritBat wanted, but the BritBat centre was the sector that UNPROFOR had given to them. I can talk about other action that took place in Kiseljak or in Kakanj. These were actions that took place outside of the BritBat territory. That was not their area of responsibility. This document was done by the BritBat commander with the original purpose of showing that for him the Busovaca Commission originally should to be concerned with occupying the situation -- by normalising the situation in the area. Why should BritBat go into other sectors? Tell me that? Other sectors would be under the control of other elements. You should not look at this document as being one -- as being one which limits the cease-fire. I can tell you that the cease-fire for the entire -- was for the entire operational zone and that is what we did. We worked on the entire operational zone, including all the UNPROFOR units that were part of that operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, during your tour, did you ever learn what had precipitated the conflict in Busovaca in January -- late January, 1993? Did you ever learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned it, the conflict -- among other people, the Croatian interpreter who was my main interpreter and who came from Busovaca lost two of his brothers during that well-known conflict. I also had heard from some of my Muslim interpreters that, yes -- about what happened. So I did understand some of what had happened. My intention was not in order to construct something from the past but to start with a cease-fire. I knew it would be difficult because there was animosity, very clearly so, whenever the two ethnic groups could meet because confidence had disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever learn as a result of your briefings and interviews and meetings whether, during the conflict in Busovaca, which began in late January 1993, whether Colonel Blaskic was in Busovaca or was cut off in the Kiseljak enclave on the other side of the strip of land from Kacuni to Bilalovac which was controlled by the BiH Army. Did you ever learn the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the annex to Exhibit 286, which should be before you, that is the last page. First of all, is it accurate or are there any errors in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that there are some errors. If you look at what was on the ground, things changed throughout the period that the Commission met. Things changed, but essentially that is what took place. I can tell you among other things that the BritBat was not always there. At the end it was not there at all. I can tell you at the end that the troops that represented the British were not troops that -- that came specifically from BritBat but rather from the British contingent. So, there were changes that took place. The reason I showed this document to the attorney who asked me the question was to show that this would give us an idea of how the Commission was structured.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it central to the design of the Commission, both at the co-ordinating committee level and at the actual Joint Commission level, that there be some symmetry or equality between the BiH Army representative or representatives and the HVO representative or representatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is what they wanted to do, that the people who were on the Commission would have as much authority as the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, the BiH Army representative on the actual Commission was Mr. Merdan; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was his rank? Was he a general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I always called him Mr. Merdan, but I think he was a general, brigadier-general, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What is Mr. Nakic's rank within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I later learned that Mr. Nakic was not -- was not a professional officer, that he was an individual, but what was important for me, since I knew that Colonel Blaskic's career, when I compare it to General Hadzihuseinovic at the beginning of the conflict that Blaskic was a captain and Hadzihuseinovic was already at the point of becoming a general. For me that was not terribly important. What I was more interested in was that we had before us two individuals with the same level of authority within their authorities -- distant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: General Merdan, by contrast, was he a career JNA officer, that is JNA, former Yugoslav National Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what I was told and what I learned, I think that General Merdan was not an infantry or an army officer, but that he had had a career at some point in the Yugoslav navy. At least that is what I was told at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As an officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Absolutely, as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me now ask you about your visit to Skradno. Do you have that subject-matter in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I explained to the Trial Chamber I have a very clear recollection of all the activities that took place in Skradno. If you are speaking about a date, I would have to check the reports in my documents. If you are speaking about what took place in Skradno, I have a very clear recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there HVO soldiers guarding the village when you visited the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason I am hesitating is that I have to tell you honestly that there were people wearing uniforms who were guarding the village. They said that they were from the police, but, as you know, both the BiH Army and the HVO used military police and regular police, but there were policemen who were guarding the entrance to the village of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you are not able to tell us today whether they were military police or civil police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. But what I can tell you is that the representatives who were with us from the HVO had visited that village, never let me think that they were not responsible for those people or that in one way or another they were not in a position to influence them. You see, that is what is important and that is what I considered important. Had there been a problem, had there been a lack of authority, I would have expected that the people who represented the HVO authorities would have said to me that these people are not under our control, but it was never said, it was never done, so I always assumed that when I would investigate into -- investigate a protest from Skradno, that those people would tell me, one way or another, now that they were in control of those police, or were not. There were several protests about Skradno and it was -- and we were never told later that Skradno was a sector that they were not concerned with. In fact, I even saw improvements which therefore let me assume that there was some type of chain of command or some type of information that was eventually disseminated amongst those people. I told them the first time I went there the people had been forced to line up against the walls of their houses and to go through a mock execution. As far as I can remember those incidents did not take place again, therefore for me there was already some improvement. It was clear that some of the information had reached there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you still have another question, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think this would be a convenient time to break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume tomorrow I think at 2.30, but there is a hearing first on another aspect of the Blaskic trial, then subsequently we will continue with the cross-examination of Colonel Landry. The court stands adjourned and we will resume tomorrow at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: on Wednesday, 22nd April 1998)
